nodes.name: Gaussian binomial coefficients
nodes.statement: The Gaussian binomial coefficients are defined by \begin{equation} \dbinom{n}{r}_q = \begin{cases} \frac{(1-q^n)(1-q^{n-1})\cdots(1-q^{n-r+1})}{(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^r)} & \text{if $r\le n$}\\ 0 & \text{if $r > n$}, \end{cases} \end{equation} where with $\mid q \mid < 1$ .
nodes.statement_short: Defines the $q$-analogue $\dbinom{n}{r}_q$ of the binomial coefficient as a ratio of $q$-shifted factorials, zero when $r>n$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial recurrence identity
nodes.statement: These coefficients satisfy the identity \begin{equation} \dbinom{n}{r}_q = q^r \dbinom{n-1}{r}_q + \dbinom{n-1}{r-1}_q. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pascal-type recurrence for the Gaussian binomial coefficients, with a $q^r$ weight on one term.
nodes.origin_citation: Kac & Cheung, Quantum calculus (2002)

nodes.name: Beta function
nodes.statement: The beta function is defined as: \begin{equation} B(p,q) = \int_{0}^1 x^{p-1} (1-x)^{1-q}dx, \quad \textrm{for}\quad Re(p), Re(q)>0. \end{equation} We have \begin{equation} B(p,q) =\frac{\Gamma (p) \Gamma (q)}{\Gamma{(p+q)}}. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Incomplete beta function
nodes.statement: The incomplete beta function is defined as \begin{equation} B(x,p,q) = \int_{0}^x t^{p-1} (1-t)^{1-q}dt, \quad \textrm{for}\quad Re(p), Re(q)>0. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Regularized incomplete beta function
nodes.statement: The regularized incomplete beta function is defined as \begin{equation} I_x(p,q) = \frac{B(x,p,q)}{B(p,q)}. \end{equation} In particular, $I_x(p,1)=x^p$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Upper and lower incomplete gamma functions
nodes.statement: The upper and lower incomplete gamma functions are defined as \begin{equation} \Gamma(n,x) = \int_{x}^\infty t^{n-1} e^{-t}dt\quad \textrm{and} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \gamma(n,x) = \int_{0}^x t^{n-1} e^{-t}dt \quad \textrm{respectively}. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung
nodes.definiendum: upper and lower incomplete gamma functions

nodes.name: Kummer's confluent hyper-geometric functions
nodes.statement: Kummer's confluent hyper-geometric functions $_{1}F_{1}(a;c;x)$ and $U(a;c;x)$ are defined as below \begin{equation} _{1}F_{1}(a;c;x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(a)_n}{(c)_n} \frac{x^n}{n!},\quad c\ne 0,-1,-2,\cdots \textrm{and} \end{equation} \begin{equation} U(a;c;x) = \frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi c)}\left(\frac{_{1}F_{1}(a;c;x)}{\Gamma(c)\Gamma(1+a-c)}-x^{1-c}\frac{_{1}F_{1}(1+a-c;2-c;x)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(2-c)}\right), \end{equation} \begin{equation} -\pi<arg (x) \leq \pi.\nonumber \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Defines $_1F_1(a;c;x)$ by its hypergeometric series and $U(a;c;x)$ as the standard reflection combination of two $_1F_1$'s.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Generalized Laguerre polynomials
nodes.statement: The generalized Laguerre polynomials are defined as \begin{eqnarray} L_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x) &=& \sum_{m=0}^n (-1)^m \dbinom{n+\alpha}{n-m}\frac{x^m}{m!}\\ &=& \dbinom{n+\alpha}{n} {}_{1}F_{1}(-n;\alpha+1;x). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Defines $L_n^{(\alpha)}(x)$ by a finite alternating sum and equivalently through $_1F_1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Space $C_\alpha$
nodes.statement: A real function $f(x)$, $x>0$, is said to be in space $C_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, if there exists a real number $p (>\alpha)$, such that $f(x)=x^p f_1(x) $ where $f_1(x)\in C[0,\infty)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung
differentia: there exists a real number $p (>\alpha)$, such that $f(x)=x^p f_1(x) $ where $f_1(x)\in C[0,\infty)$

nodes.name: Space $C^m_\alpha$
nodes.statement: A real function $f(x)$, $x > 0$, is said to be in space $C^m_\alpha$, $m\in\mathbb{N}\cup \{0\}$, if $ f^{(m)} \in C_\alpha$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Riemann-Liouville fractional integral
nodes.statement: Let $f\in C_\alpha $ and $\alpha \geq -1$, then the (left-sided) Riemann-Liouville integral of order $\mu, \mu> 0 $ is given by \begin{equation} I^\mu f(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\mu)} \int_{0}^t (t-\tau)^{\mu-1}f(\tau)d\tau,\quad t>0. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Caputo fractional derivative
nodes.statement: The (left sided) Caputo fractional derivative of $f, f \in C_{-1}^m, m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$, is defined as: \begin{eqnarray} D^\mu f(t)&=&\frac{d^m}{ dt^m} f(t),\quad \mu = m \nonumber\\ &=& I^{m-\mu}\frac{d^m}{ dt^m} f(t),\quad {m-1} <\mu <m,\quad m\in \mathbb{N}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Caputo derivative of order $\mu$: the ordinary $m$-th derivative when $\mu=m$, otherwise $I^{m-\mu}$ applied to it.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Fractional integral of a power and the $I^\alpha D^\alpha$ composition
nodes.statement: Note that for $0\le m-1 < \alpha \le m$ and $\beta>-1$ \begin{eqnarray} I^\alpha (x-b)^\beta &=&\frac{\Gamma{(\beta+1)}}{ \Gamma{(\beta+\alpha+1)}} (x-b)^{\beta+\alpha},\nonumber\\ \left(I^\alpha D^\alpha f\right)(t)&=& f(t)-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} f^{(k)}(0)\frac{t^k}{k!}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Gives $I^\alpha (x-b)^\beta$ in closed form and the inversion rule $I^\alpha D^\alpha f = f$ minus its Taylor head.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Identity $\Gamma(1,x) = e^{-x}$
nodes.statement: $\Gamma(1,x) = e^{-x}$
nodes.statement_short: Upper incomplete gamma at order $1$ reduces to $e^{-x}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Recurrence for $\Gamma(n+1,x)$
nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n+1,x) = n \Gamma(n,x)+ x^n e^x$
nodes.statement_short: Order-raising recurrence for the upper incomplete gamma function.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Recurrence for $\gamma(n+1,x)$
nodes.statement: $\gamma(n+1,x) = n \gamma(n,x) - x^n e^{-x}$
nodes.statement_short: Order-raising recurrence for the lower incomplete gamma function.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Finite-sum form of $\Gamma(n+1,x)$
nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n+1,x) = n! e^{-x} \sum_{m=0}^n\frac{x^m}{m!}$
nodes.statement_short: Closed finite-sum evaluation of $\Gamma(n+1,x)$ at integer order.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Finite-sum form of $\gamma(n+1,x)$
nodes.statement: $\gamma(n+1,x) = n!\left(1- e^{-x} \sum_{m=0}^n\frac{x^m}{m!}\right)$
nodes.statement_short: Closed finite-sum evaluation of $\gamma(n+1,x)$ at integer order.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.name: Laguerre series for $\Gamma(n,x)$
nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n,x) = e^{-x}x^n \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{L_{m}^{(n)}(x)}{m+1}$
nodes.statement_short: Expands $\Gamma(n,x)$ in generalized Laguerre polynomials.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n,x) = x^n e^{-x}U(1; 1+n; x)$
nodes.statement_short: Expresses $\Gamma(n,x)$ through $U(1;1+n;x)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus, Oberhettinger & Soni; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas, Srivastava & Trujillo; Podlubny; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev; Kac & Cheung

nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n,x) = e^{-x}U(1-n; 1-n; x)$

nodes.name: Daftardar-Gejji and Jafari Method (DJM)
nodes.statement: Suppose that given problem can be transformed to the model equation \begin{equation} u= f + L(u) + N(u), \end{equation} where $L$ and $N$ are linear and nonlinear operators respectively and $f$ is known function.\\ In this case, the DJM provides the solution in the form of series \begin{equation} u= \sum_{i=0}^\infty u_i. \end{equation} where $u_0=f,\; u_1=N(u_0)\;$ and \begin{equation} u_{n+1} = N\left(\sum_{j=0}^n u_j\right)- N\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} u_j\right), \quad n=1, 2, \cdots. \\ \end{equation} Usually, the k-term approximate solution $u= \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} u_i$ is used to approximate the exact solution.
nodes.statement_short: Decomposition iteration for $u=f+L(u)+N(u)$: take $u_0=f$, $u_1=N(u_0)$ and successive differences of $N$ on partial sums, then sum the series.
nodes.origin_citation: Daftardar-Gejji & Jafari 2006
input: $L$ and $N$ are linear and nonlinear operators respectively and $f$ is known function
output: the solution in the form of series

nodes.name: Transform to the model equation
nodes.statement: Suppose that given problem can be transformed to the model equation \begin{equation} u= f + L(u) + N(u), \end{equation} where $L$ and $N$ are linear and nonlinear operators respectively and $f$ is known function.
nodes.statement_short: Recast the given problem in the canonical form $u=f+L(u)+N(u)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Daftardar-Gejji & Jafari 2006

nodes.name: Posit the series ansatz
nodes.statement: In this case, the DJM provides the solution in the form of series \begin{equation} u= \sum_{i=0}^\infty u_i. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Seek the solution as an infinite series $u=\sum_i u_i$.
nodes.origin_citation: Daftardar-Gejji & Jafari 2006

nodes.name: Generate the iterates
nodes.statement: where $u_0=f,\; u_1=N(u_0)\;$ and \begin{equation} u_{n+1} = N\left(\sum_{j=0}^n u_j\right)- N\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} u_j\right), \quad n=1, 2, \cdots. \\ \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set $u_0=f$, $u_1=N(u_0)$, then update by successive differences of $N$ on partial sums.
nodes.origin_citation: Daftardar-Gejji & Jafari 2006

nodes.name: Truncate to $k$ terms
nodes.statement: Usually, the k-term approximate solution $u= \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} u_i$ is used to approximate the exact solution.
nodes.statement_short: Return the $k$-term partial sum as the approximate solution.
nodes.origin_citation: Daftardar-Gejji & Jafari 2006

nodes.name: Convergence of the DJM series under a uniform derivative bound
nodes.statement: \cite{CONV} If $N$ is $C^{(\infty)}$ in a neighborhood of $y_0$ and $\left\|N^{(n)}(y_0) \right\| \leq L$, for any $n$ and for some real $L>0$ and $\left\|y_i\right\| \leq M <\frac{1}{e}$, $i=1,2,\cdots,$ then the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is absolutely convergent to $N$ and moreover, \begin{equation*} \left\|G_n\right\| \leq L M^n e^{n-1} (e-1), \quad n=1,2,\cdots. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Uniformly bounded derivatives plus $\|y_i\|<1/e$ give absolute convergence of the DJM series with a geometric-type term bound.
nodes.origin_citation: Bhalekar & Daftardar-Gejji 2011
assumptions: If $N$ is $C^{(\infty)}$ in a neighborhood of $y_0$
$\left\|N^{(n)}(y_0) \right\| \leq L$, for any $n$ and for some real $L>0$
conclusions: the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is absolutely convergent to $N$

nodes.name: Convergence of the DJM series under $\|N^{(n)}(y_0)\|\le e^{-1}$
nodes.statement: \cite{CONV} If $N$ is $C^{(\infty)}$ and $\left\|N^{(n)}(y_0) \right\| \leq M \leq e^{-1}$, $\forall n$, then the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is absolutely convergent to $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivative norms bounded by $e^{-1}$ already force absolute convergence of the DJM series.
nodes.origin_citation: Bhalekar & Daftardar-Gejji 2011
conclusions: the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is absolutely convergent to $N$

nodes.name: Proportional delay as a time-dependent delay
nodes.statement: The equation \begin{equation} y'(t) = f\left(t, y(t), y(pt)\right), \end{equation} is a particular case of time dependent delay differential equation (DDE) \begin{equation} y'(t) = f\left(t, y(t), y\left(t-\tau(t)\right)\right)\quad \textrm{with}\quad\tau(t)=(1-p)t. \end{equation} The existence and uniqueness theorems for (\ref{6.2.4}) are described in \cite{Bellen} as below.
nodes.statement_short: Notes that proportional delay $y(pt)$ is the special case $\tau(t)=(1-p)t$ of a time-dependent-delay DDE.

nodes.name: Local existence
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Local existence})\\ Consider the equation \begin{eqnarray} y'(t)&=& f\left(t, y(t), y\left(t-\tau(t)\right)\right),\quad t_0 \leq t < t_f,\nonumber\\ y(t_0)&=& y_0, \end{eqnarray} and assume that the function $f(t,u,v)$ is continuous on $A \subseteq [t_0,t_f)\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^m$ and locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to u and v. Moreover, assume that the delay function $\tau(t)\geq 0$ is continuous in $[t_0,t_f)$, $\tau(t_0)=0$ and, for some $\xi > 0 $, $t-\tau(t) > t_0$ in the interval $(t_0, t_0+\xi]$. Then the problem (\ref{pro1}) has a unique solution in $[t_0,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta >0$ and this solution depends continuously on the initial data.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity plus local Lipschitz dependence and a delay vanishing at $t_0$ give a unique local solution depending continuously on the data.
nodes.origin_citation: Bellen & Zennaro 2013
assumptions: assume that the function $f(t,u,v)$ is continuous on $A \subseteq [t_0,t_f)\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^m$ and locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to u and v
assume that the delay function $\tau(t)\geq 0$ is continuous in $[t_0,t_f)$, $\tau(t_0)=0$ and, for some $\xi > 0 $, $t-\tau(t) > t_0$ in the interval $(t_0, t_0+\xi]$
conclusions: Then the problem (\ref{pro1}) has a unique solution in $[t_0,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta >0$ and this solution depends continuously on the initial data.

nodes.name: Global existence
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Global existence})\\ Under the hypothesis of Theorem \ref{th1}, if the unique maximal solution of (\ref{pro1}) is bounded, then it exist on the entire interval $[t_0,t_f)$.
nodes.statement_short: A bounded maximal solution extends over the whole interval $[t_0,t_f)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Bellen & Zennaro 2013
assumptions: if the unique maximal solution of (\ref{pro1}) is bounded
conclusions: then it exist on the entire interval $[t_0,t_f)$

nodes.name: Linear DDE with proportional delay and unit initial value
nodes.statement: Consider the differential equation with proportional delay \begin{equation} y'(x) = ay(x)+ by(q x),\quad y(0)= 1, \end{equation} where $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the initial value problem $y'(x)=ay(x)+by(qx)$, $y(0)=1$, with $0<q<1$.

nodes.name: Standing parameter assumptions
nodes.statement: where $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Throughout, the delay factor satisfies $0<q<1$ and the coefficients $a,b$ are real.

nodes.name: Equivalent Volterra integral equation
nodes.statement: Integrating (\ref{6.3.1}), we get \begin{equation} y(x)= 1 + \int_{0}^{x}\left( ay(t)+ by(qt)\right)dt \end{equation} which is of the form Eq.(\ref{1.1.1}).
nodes.statement_short: Integrating the DDE gives $y(x)=1+\int_0^x(ay(t)+by(qt))dt$, which matches the DJM model form.

nodes.name: DJM iterates $y_n(x)$
nodes.statement:
Applying DJM, we obtain  egin{eqnarray} y_0(x) &=& 1 ,
onumber\ y_1(x)&=& \int_{0}^{x}\left( ay_0(t)+ by_0(q t)ight)dt
onumber\ &=& (a+b) rac{x}{1!},
onumber\ y_2(x)&=& \int_{0}^{x}\left( ay_1(t)+ by_1(q t)ight)dt
onumber\ &=&\int_{0}^{x}\left(a (a+b)t + b (a+b)tqight)dt
onumber\ &=& (a+b)(a+bq) rac{x^2}{2!},
onumber \end{eqnarray}  egin{eqnarray} y_3(x)&=& \int_{0}^{x}\left(ay_2(t)+ by_2(q t)ight)dt
onumber\ &=& (a+b)(a+bq)(a+bq^2) rac{x^3}{3!},
onumber\ &\vdots& 
onumber\ y_n(x)&=&  rac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight), \quad n=1,2,3\cdots. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Successive DJM iterates evaluate to $y_n(x)=\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(a+bq^j)$.

nodes.name: DJM series solution of the DDE
nodes.statement: $\therefore$ The DJM solution of (\ref{6.3.1}) is \begin{eqnarray} y(x) &=& y_0(x)+y_1(x)+y_2(x)+\cdots\nonumber\\ &=& 1 + (a+b)\frac{x}{1!} + (a+b)(a+bq)\frac{x^2}{2!}+\cdots\nonumber\\ y(x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Summing the iterates yields $y(x)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(a+bq^j)$.

nodes.name: Ramanujan function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)$
nodes.statement: The power series solution (\ref{6.3.3}) of DDE (\ref{6.3.1}) generates a novel special function \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{equation} We call this function as Ramanujan function in the memory of S. Ramanujan \cite{Kanigel}.
nodes.statement_short: Names the series $1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(a+bq^j)$ the Ramanujan function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)$.

nodes.name: Infinite radius of convergence of $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: If $0<q<1$, then the power series \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) \end{equation} has infinite radius of convergence.
nodes.statement_short: For $0<q<1$ the Ramanujan series is entire.

nodes.name: Proof of infinite radius of convergence
nodes.statement:
Suppose  egin{equation} a_n = rac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight),\quad n=1,2,\cdots. \end{equation} If $R$ is radius of convergence of (ef{6.5.0}) then by using ratio test \cite{Apostal}  egin{eqnarray}  rac{1}{R}=\lim_{n	o\infty}\left|  rac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}ight| &=&\lim_{n	o\infty}\left|  rac{  rac{1}{{(n+1)!}}\prod_{j=0}^{n}\left(a+bq^jight)}{  rac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight)}ight| 
onumber\ &=& \lim_{n	o\infty} \left|  rac{a}{(n+1)} +  rac{bq^n}{(n+1)}ight| 
onumber\ \Rightarrow rac{1}{R}&=& 0 \quad ( ecause 0<q<1)
onumber \end{eqnarray} Thus the series has infinite radius of convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio test on $a_n=\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^j)$; the ratio tends to $0$ because $0<q<1$.

nodes.name: Introduce the coefficient sequence
nodes.statement: Suppose \begin{equation} a_n =\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right),\quad n=1,2,\cdots. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Name the series coefficients $a_n$.

nodes.name: Apply the ratio test
nodes.statement: If $R$ is radius of convergence of (\ref{6.5.0}) then by using ratio test \cite{Apostal} \begin{eqnarray} \frac{1}{R}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| &=&\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \frac{ \frac{1}{{(n+1)!}}\prod_{j=0}^{n}\left(a+bq^j\right)}{ \frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)}\right| \nonumber\\ &=& \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{a}{(n+1)} + \frac{bq^n}{(n+1)}\right| \nonumber\\ \Rightarrow\frac{1}{R}&=& 0 \quad (\because 0<q<1)
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|=0$ using $0<q<1$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus the series has infinite radius of convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude that $R=\infty$.

nodes.name: Absolute and uniform convergence of $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: The power series (\ref{6.3.4}) is absolutely convergent for all x, if $0<q<1$ and hence it is uniformly convergent on any compact interval on $\mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: The power series (\ref{6.3.4}) is absolutely convergent for all x
hence it is uniformly convergent on any compact interval on $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Derivative of $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x)$
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N} \cup\{0\} $, we have \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x)= a q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) + b q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{m+1}x). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiating $\mathcal{R}$ at the scaled argument $q^m x$ reproduces the DDE: $aq^m\mathcal{R}(q^m x)+bq^m\mathcal{R}(q^{m+1}x)$.
conclusions: \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x)= a q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) + b q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{m+1}x).

nodes.name: Proof of the first-derivative relation
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ &=& q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=2}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n}}{{n}!}\prod_{j=0}^{n}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n}(a+bq^n)}{{n}!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& aq^m \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ && + bq^m \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^{m+1}x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) &=& a q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) + b q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{m+1}x) \end{eqnarray*} Hence the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Term-by-term differentiation of the series, then re-indexing and splitting the factor $(a+bq^n)$.

nodes.name: $m$-th derivative of $\mathcal{R}$ via Gaussian binomial coefficients
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$, we have \begin{equation} \frac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x), \end{equation} where $\dbinom{m}{r}_q$ is the Gaussian binomial coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: The $m$-th derivative of $\mathcal{R}$ is a Gaussian-binomial-weighted combination of $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x)$ for $0\le r\le m$.

nodes.name: Proof of the $m$-th derivative formula
nodes.statement:
We prove the result by induction hypothesis on $m$.\ From Theorem ef{6.1.3}, the result is true for $m=1$. \ Suppose,  egin{equation}  rac{d^{m-1}}{dx^{m-1}}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x). \end{equation} Consider,\  egin{eqnarray}  rac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=&  rac{d}{dx} \left( rac{d^{m-1}}{dx^{m-1}}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)ight)\ &=&  rac{d}{dx} \left( \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x)ight)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r  rac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x). \end{eqnarray} Using Theorem [ef{6.1.3}], we have  egin{eqnarray*}  rac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r 
onumber\ &&\left( a q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx) + b q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{r+1}x)ight)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ &&+ \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} q^k \dbinom{m-1}{k}_q a^{m-(k+1)} b^{k+1} \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{k+1}x) \end{eqnarray*}  egin{eqnarray*} &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=1}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)
onumber\ && - q^{\dbinom{m}{2}} q^m \dbinom{m-1}{m}_q b^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) \ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) 
onumber\ && - \dbinom{m-1}{-1}_q a^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q, x) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \left(q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q + \dbinom{m-1}{r-1}_q ight) a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx). \end{eqnarray*} Using identity (ef{6.1.2}),  egin{equation}  rac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx), \end{equation} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $m$, using the first-derivative relation and the Gaussian binomial recurrence.

nodes.name: Set up the induction
nodes.statement: We prove the result by induction hypothesis on $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Announce induction on the derivative order $m$.

nodes.name: Base case $m=1$
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{6.1.3}, the result is true for $m=1$.
nodes.statement_short: The base case is exactly the first-derivative theorem.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Suppose, \begin{equation} \frac{d^{m-1}}{dx^{m-1}}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume the formula holds at order $m-1$.

nodes.name: Differentiate the inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Consider,\\ \begin{eqnarray} \frac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left(\frac{d^{m-1}}{dx^{m-1}}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\right)\\ &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left( \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x)\right)\\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the order-$(m-1)$ expression term by term.

nodes.name: Substitute the first-derivative relation and re-index
nodes.statement:
Using Theorem [ef{6.1.3}], we have  egin{eqnarray*}  rac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r 
onumber\ &&\left( a q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx) + b q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{r+1}x)ight)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ &&+ \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} q^k \dbinom{m-1}{k}_q a^{m-(k+1)} b^{k+1} \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{k+1}x) \end{eqnarray*}  egin{eqnarray*} &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=1}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)
onumber\ && - q^{\dbinom{m}{2}} q^m \dbinom{m-1}{m}_q b^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) \ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) 
onumber\ && - \dbinom{m-1}{-1}_q a^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q, x) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \left(q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q + \dbinom{m-1}{r-1}_q ight) a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Insert the first-derivative theorem, shift the second sum's index and merge the two sums.

nodes.name: Apply the Gaussian binomial recurrence
nodes.statement: Using identity (\ref{6.1.2}), \begin{equation} \frac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx), \end{equation} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse $q^r\dbinom{m-1}{r}_q+\dbinom{m-1}{r-1}_q$ into $\dbinom{m}{r}_q$.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial double-series form of $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, we have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}, \end{equation} where $\dbinom{n}{r}_q$ is the Gaussian binomial coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: Expanding the product gives $\mathcal{R}$ as a double sum with Gaussian binomial coefficients.

nodes.name: Proof of the double-series form
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{equation} Using the $q$- binomial theorem \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r, \end{equation} defined in \cite{Richard}, we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r\nonumber\\ \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray} Hence the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the $q$-binomial theorem for $\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^j)$ into the defining series.

nodes.name: Recall the defining series
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Start from the definition of $\mathcal{R}$.

nodes.name: Invoke the $q$-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: Using the $q$- binomial theorem \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r, \end{equation} defined in \cite{Richard},
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^j)$ by the $q$-binomial theorem.

nodes.name: Substitute and conclude
nodes.statement: we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r\nonumber\\ \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray} Hence the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Insert the expansion and rearrange into the stated double sum.

nodes.name: $q$-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: Using the $q$- binomial theorem \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r, \end{equation} defined in \cite{Richard}
nodes.statement_short: $\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(a+bq^j)$ expands as a Gaussian-binomial-weighted sum of $a^{n-r}b^r$.
nodes.origin_citation: Richard P. Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics (1997)

nodes.name: Exponential bounds on $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, $a\ge 0$ and $b\ge 0$, the function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)$ satisfies the following inequality \begin{equation} e^{ax}\le \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\le e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For nonnegative $a,b$ the Ramanujan function is squeezed between $e^{ax}$ and $e^{(a+b)x}$ on $[0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the exponential bounds
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^j)$ above by $(a+b)^n$ and below by $a^n$, then sum termwise.

nodes.name: Upper bound on the product
nodes.statement_short: Use $a+bq^j\le a+b$ and sum to obtain the upper bound $e^{(a+b)x}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the product
nodes.statement: Similarly, we have \begin{eqnarray} a^n &\le& \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) \nonumber\\ \Rightarrow e^{ax} &\le& \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) ,\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Use $a^n\le\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^j)$ to obtain the lower bound $e^{ax}$.

nodes.name: Combine the two bounds
nodes.statement: From (\ref{6.5.1}) and (\ref{6.5.2}), we get \begin{equation} e^{ax}\le \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\le e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two estimates into the stated two-sided inequality.

nodes.name: Integral $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt = \Gamma (1, x)\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The tail exponential integral of $\mathcal{R}$ factors as $\Gamma(1,x)$ times a Gaussian-binomial triple sum.

nodes.name: Proof of the tail integral formula
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \Gamma(n+1,x)\\ &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} n! e^{-x}\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\\ &=& e^{-x}\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\\ \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)dt &=& \Gamma (1, x)\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the series termwise against $e^{-t}$, evaluate $\Gamma(n+1,x)$ by its finite-sum identity, then apply the $q$-binomial expansion.

nodes.name: Integral $\int_0^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The truncated exponential integral of $\mathcal{R}$ splits into a constant double sum minus a $\Gamma(1,x)$-weighted triple sum.
conclusions: \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right).

nodes.name: Proof of the truncated integral formula
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{0}^xe^{-t} dt + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \gamma(n+1,x)\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} n!\left( 1-e^{-x}\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\\ &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && - e^{-x}\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r\frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\;(\textrm{From (\ref{6.5.5})})\\ \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration produces $\gamma(n+1,x)$, expanded by its finite-sum identity and then by the $q$-binomial theorem.

nodes.name: Relation of $\int_0^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$ with Kummer's $_1F_1$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=&1 + \Gamma (1, x)\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(1; n+1; x) - \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\right)\\ &=& 1 -\Gamma (1, x) \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(n; n+1; -x). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Two equivalent expressions for the truncated integral of $\mathcal{R}$ in terms of $_1F_1(1;n+1;x)$ and $_1F_1(n;n+1;-x)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the $_1F_1$ relations

nodes.name: Integrate the series termwise
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{0}^xe^{-t} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \gamma(n+1,x)\\ \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate term by term to reach $\gamma(n+1,x)$.

nodes.name: Apply the $\gamma$ recurrence
nodes.statement: Using the property (\ref{6.1.8}) in Section \textbf{\ref{6.1.4}}, we have \begin{eqnarray} &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \left(n\gamma(n,x)-x^n e^{-x}\right)\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} \left(\gamma(n,x)\right)-e^{-x}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Lower the order via $\gamma(n+1,x)=n\gamma(n,x)-x^ne^{-x}$.

nodes.name: Substitute the $_1F_1(1;n+1;x)$ representation
nodes.statement: Using the relation (\ref{6.1.14}) in Section \textbf{\ref{6.1.4}}, we get \begin{eqnarray} &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} \left( n^{-1} x^n e^{-x}{}_1F_{1}(1; n+1; x)\right) \nonumber\\ &&-e^{-x}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\\ \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt&=& 1 + \Gamma (1, x)\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(1; n+1; x) - \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\right)\nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\gamma(n,x)$ by its $_1F_1(1;n+1;x)$ form.

nodes.name: Substitute the $_1F_1(n;n+1;-x)$ representation
nodes.statement: Again using the relation (\ref{6.1.15}) in \textbf{\ref{6.1.4}}, we get \begin{equation} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt= 1 -\Gamma (1, x) \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(n; n+1; -x) \nonumber \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat with the alternative $_1F_1$ form to obtain the second identity.

nodes.name: Relation of $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$ with Kummer's $U$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt&=& \Gamma (1, x) + x\Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} U(1; 1+n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right).\\ &=&\Gamma (1, x) + \Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} U(1-n; 1-n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Two equivalent expressions for the tail integral of $\mathcal{R}$ via $U(1;1+n;x)$ and $U(1-n;1-n;x)$.
conclusions: \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt&=& \Gamma (1, x) + x\Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} U(1; 1+n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right).\\ &=&\Gamma (1, x) + \Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} U(1-n; 1-n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right).

nodes.statement:

nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration to $\Gamma(n+1,x)$, then the $\Gamma$ identities and the two $U$ representations.

nodes.name: Integrate the series termwise
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \Gamma(n+1,x)\\ \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate term by term to reach $\Gamma(n+1,x)$.

nodes.name: Apply the $\Gamma$ identities
nodes.statement: Using the properties (\ref{6.1.5}) and (\ref{6.1.7}) in Section \textbf{\ref{6.1.4}}, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \Gamma (1, x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \left(n\Gamma(n,x)+x^n e^x\right)\\ &=& \Gamma (1, x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} \left(\Gamma(n,x)\right)+e^x\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Use $\Gamma(1,x)=e^{-x}$ and the raising recurrence to lower the order.

nodes.name: Substitute the $U(1;1+n;x)$ representation
nodes.statement: Using the relation (\ref{6.1.16}), we get \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \Gamma (1, x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} \left( x^n e^{-x}U(1; 1+n; x)\right) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right)\\ \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt&=& \Gamma (1, x) + x\Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} U(1; 1+n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\Gamma(n,x)$ by its $U(1;1+n;x)$ form.

nodes.name: Substitute the $U(1-n;1-n;x)$ representation
nodes.statement: Again using the relation (\ref{6.1.17}), we get \begin{eqnarray} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt&=& \Gamma (1, x) + \Gamma (1, x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{(n-1)!} U(1-n; 1-n; x) \nonumber\\ && + e^x\left(\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)-1\right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat with the alternative $U$ form to obtain the second identity.

nodes.name: Relation of $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$ with generalized Laguerre polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Three equivalent expansions of the tail integral of $\mathcal{R}$ using $L_m^{(n)}$ and $_1F_1(-m;n+1;x)$.

nodes.name: Scaled integral $\int_0^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \int_{0}^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \gamma (1, x) + \lambda\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Scaling the argument by $\lambda$ yields a double sum of lower incomplete gamma values weighted by $(1-\lambda)^m$.

nodes.name: Proof of the scaled truncated integral
nodes.statement: We have \begin{eqnarray} \int_{0}^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt &=& 1 - e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!}\int_{0}^x e^{-t}(\lambda t)^n dt\nonumber\\ &=& \gamma(1,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \gamma(n+1,\lambda x). \end{eqnarray} By using the property \cite{Gautschi} $\gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$, we get \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \gamma (1, x) + \lambda\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration to $\gamma(n+1,\lambda x)$, then Gautschi's scaling expansion for the incomplete gamma function.

nodes.name: Integrate termwise at the scaled argument
nodes.statement: We have \begin{eqnarray} \int_{0}^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt &=& 1 - e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!}\int_{0}^x e^{-t}(\lambda t)^n dt\nonumber\\ &=& \gamma(1,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \gamma(n+1,\lambda x). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration produces $\gamma(n+1,\lambda x)$.

nodes.name: Apply Gautschi's scaling expansion
nodes.statement: By using the property \cite{Gautschi} $\gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$, we get \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^x e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \gamma (1, x) + \lambda\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\gamma(n,\lambda x)$ in $\gamma(n+m,x)$ with $(1-\lambda)^m$ weights.

nodes.name: Gautschi scaling expansion for $\gamma(n,\lambda x)$
nodes.statement: $\gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$
nodes.statement_short: Expands the lower incomplete gamma at a scaled argument in a $(1-\lambda)^m$-weighted series.
nodes.origin_citation: Gautschi, Harris & Temme 2003

nodes.name: Scaled tail integral $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \Gamma (1, x) + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\Gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Upper-incomplete-gamma analogue of the previous scaling identity.

nodes.name: Proof of the scaled tail integral
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!}\int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}(\lambda t)^n dt\nonumber\\ &=& \Gamma(1,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \Gamma(n+1,\lambda x). \end{eqnarray} By using the property \cite{Gautschi} $\Gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\Gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$, we obtain \begin{equation*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \Gamma (1, x) + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\Gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration to $\Gamma(n+1,\lambda x)$, then Gautschi's scaling expansion for the upper incomplete gamma function.

nodes.name: Integrate termwise at the scaled argument
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!}\int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}(\lambda t)^n dt\nonumber\\ &=& \Gamma(1,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \Gamma(n+1,\lambda x). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise integration produces $\Gamma(n+1,\lambda x)$.

nodes.name: Apply Gautschi's scaling expansion
nodes.statement: By using the property \cite{Gautschi} $\Gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\Gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$, we obtain \begin{equation*} \int_{x}^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,\lambda t)dt = \Gamma (1, x) + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=0}^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {\lambda^n}{n!} \frac {\Gamma(n+m+1, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\Gamma(n,\lambda x)$ in $\Gamma(n+m,x)$ with $(1-\lambda)^m$ weights.

nodes.name: Gautschi scaling expansion for $\Gamma(n,\lambda x)$
nodes.statement: $\Gamma(n,\lambda x) = \lambda^n\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{\Gamma(n+m, x)}{m!}(1-\lambda)^m$
nodes.statement_short: Expands the upper incomplete gamma at a scaled argument in a $(1-\lambda)^m$-weighted series.
nodes.origin_citation: Gautschi, Harris & Temme 2003

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}(0,\cdot,q,\cdot)$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm a^{l}b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm a^{l}b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: With $a=0$ the second parameter can be absorbed into the argument.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm a^{l}b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm a^{l}b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}(a^m,a^m,q,x)$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^m, a^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,1,q,a^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^{-m}, \pm a^m,q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{2m},q,\pm a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^m, \pm a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{-2m},q,\pm a^mx\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^m, a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,-a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^m, -a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^{-m}, a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,-a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^{-m}, -a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,a^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Equal parameters can be normalized to $1$ by rescaling the argument.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^m, a^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,1,q,a^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^{-m}, \pm a^m,q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{2m},q,\pm a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^m, \pm a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{-2m},q,\pm a^mx\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^m, a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,-a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^m, -a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^{-m}, a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,-a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^{-m}, -a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,a^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: General parameter-normalization property of $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^l, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{-l} b^m,q,a^lx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^l b^{-m}, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{-l} b^{2m},q,a^l b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{-l} b^m, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^l,q,a^{-l} b^{m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{l} b^{-m}, a^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{m-l}b^m,q,a^l b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{-l} b^{m}, a^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{l+m}b^{-m},q,a^{-l} b^{m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The first parameter can always be normalized to $1$ by rescaling the second parameter and the argument.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^l, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{-l} b^m,q,a^lx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^l b^{-m}, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{-l} b^{2m},q,a^l b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{-l} b^m, b^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^l,q,a^{-l} b^{m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{l} b^{-m}, a^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{m-l}b^m,q,a^l b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(a^{-l} b^{m}, a^m, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1, a^{l+m}b^{-m},q,a^{-l} b^{m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Representation of $\mathcal{R}$ via the incomplete beta function
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{B(x,n,1)}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrites the monomial $x^n$ in the series as $B(x,n,1)$.

nodes.name: Representation of $\mathcal{R}$ via a ratio of beta functions
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{B(x,n,1)}{B(n,1)n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrites the series coefficients as $B(x,n,1)/B(n,1)$.

nodes.name: Representation of $\mathcal{R}$ via the regularized incomplete beta function
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{I_x(n,1)}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrites the monomial $x^n$ as the regularized incomplete beta $I_x(n,1)$.

nodes.name: Contiguous special functions and contiguous relations
nodes.statement: \cite{Erdelyi} Two special functions are said to be contiguous if their parameters $a$ and $b$ differ by integers. The relations made by contiguous functions are said to be contiguous function relations.
nodes.origin_citation: Erdelyi, Magnus, Oberhettinger & Tricomi 1955
differentia: their parameters $a$ and $b$ differ by integers

nodes.name: Contiguous relation in the first parameter
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a\pm 1, b, q, x) = \mathcal{R}( 1, (a \pm 1)^{-1} b, q, (a \pm 1)x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting $a$ by $\pm1$ is absorbed by renormalizing the second parameter and the argument.

nodes.name: Contiguous relation in the second parameter
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a, b\pm 1, q, x) = \mathcal{R}( 1, a^{-1}(b \pm 1), q, ax)$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting $b$ by $\pm1$ is absorbed by renormalizing the second parameter.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}(a, b\pm 1, q, x) = \mathcal{R}( 1, a^{-1}(b \pm 1), q, ax)$.

nodes.name: Contiguous relation in both parameters
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}(a\pm 1,, b\pm 1, q, x) = \mathcal{R}( 1, (a \pm 1)^{-1}(b \pm 1), q, (a \pm 1)x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting both $a$ and $b$ by $\pm1$ is absorbed by a single renormalization.

nodes.name: Fractional DDE with proportional delay
nodes.statement: Consider the fractional delay differential equation with proportional delay \begin{equation} D^\alpha_0y(x) = ay(x)+ by(q x),\quad y(0)= 1, \end{equation} where $0<\alpha \leq 1$, $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $D^\alpha_0 y(x)=ay(x)+by(qx)$, $y(0)=1$, for $0<\alpha\le1$.

nodes.name: Equivalent fractional integral equation
nodes.statement: Equivalently \begin{equation} y(x) = 1 + I^\alpha (ay(x)+ by(q x)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The fractional IVP is equivalent to $y=1+I^\alpha(ay+by(q\cdot))$.

nodes.name: DJM series solution of the fractional DDE
nodes.statement: The DJM solution of (\ref{7.1.2}) is \begin{equation} y(x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma{(\alpha n + 1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^{\alpha j}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: DJM yields $y(x)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma(\alpha n+1)}\prod_{j<n}(a+bq^{\alpha j})$.

nodes.name: Fractional Ramanujan function $\mathcal{R}_\alpha(a,b,q,x)$
nodes.statement: We denote the series in (\ref{7.1.3}) by \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}_\alpha(a, b, q, x) =1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma{(\alpha n + 1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^{\alpha j}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Names the Mittag-Leffler-type series solving the fractional DDE $\mathcal{R}_\alpha(a,b,q,x)$.

nodes.name: Convergence of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: If $0<q<1$, then the power series \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}_\alpha(a, b, q, x) =1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma{(\alpha n + 1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^{\alpha j}\right), \end{equation} is convergent for all finite values of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: The fractional Ramanujan series converges for every finite $x$.
conclusions: \mathcal{R}_\alpha(a, b, q, x) =1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma{(\alpha n + 1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^{\alpha j}\right),
is convergent for all finite values of $x$

nodes.name: Proof of convergence of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: Result follows immediately by ratio test \begin{eqnarray*} \lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| &=& a \left|x\right|^\alpha \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac {\Gamma(\alpha n)}{\Gamma{(\alpha (n + 1))}}\\ &=& 0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Ratio test: the ratio $\Gamma(\alpha n)/\Gamma(\alpha(n+1))\to0$.

nodes.name: Analogous properties of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: \par We get following analogous properties and relations as in Section \ref{Prop} e.g.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha(0,\cdot,q,\cdot)$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(0,\pm b^{\alpha m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{\alpha m}x\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fractional analogue of the $a=0$ scaling property.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha(a^{\alpha m},a^{\alpha m},q,x)$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha m}, a^{\alpha m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1,1,q,a^{\alpha m}x\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fractional analogue of the equal-parameter normalization.

nodes.name: General parameter-normalization property of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha l}, b^{\alpha m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1, a^{-{\alpha m}} b^{\alpha m},q,a^{\alpha l}x\right)$ and so on.
nodes.statement_short: Fractional analogue of the general first-parameter normalization.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha l}, b^{\alpha m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1, a^{-{\alpha m}} b^{\alpha m},q,a^{\alpha l}x\right)$ and so on.

nodes.name: System of DDEs with proportional delay
nodes.statement: Consider the system of delay differential equation with proportional delay \begin{equation} Y'(x) = AY(x)+ BY(q x),\quad Y(0)= Y_0, \end{equation} where $0<q<1$, $A=\left(a_{ij}\right)_{n\times n}$, $B=\left(b_{ij}\right)_{n\times n}$ and $Y=$ $ \begin{bmatrix} y_1\\ y_2\\ \vdots\\ y_n \end{bmatrix}. $
nodes.statement_short: Solve the matrix initial value problem $Y'(x)=AY(x)+BY(qx)$, $Y(0)=Y_0$.

nodes.name: Equivalent integral equation for the system
nodes.statement: The equivalent integral equation is \begin{equation} Y(x)= Y_0 + \int_{0}^{x}\left( AY(t)+ BY(qt)\right)dt. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Matrix IVP recast as $Y(x)=Y_0+\int_0^x (AY(t)+BY(qt))dt$.

nodes.name: DJM iterates $Y_n(x)$ for the system
nodes.statement:
Using DJM, we obtain  egin{eqnarray} Y_1(x)&=& \int_{0}^{x}\left( AY(t)+ BY(qt)ight)dt
onumber\ &=& (A+B)Y_0 rac{x}{1!},
onumber\ Y_2(x)&=& (A+qB)(A+B)Y_0  rac{x^2}{2!},
onumber\ Y_3(x)&=& (A+q^2B)(A+qB)(A+B)Y_0  rac{x^3}{3!},
onumber\ &\vdots& 
onumber\ Y_n(x)&=& (A+q^{n-1}B)(A+q^{n-2}B)\cdots (A+B)Y_0  rac{x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Iterates are ordered matrix products $(A+q^{n-1}B)\cdots(A+B)Y_0x^n/n!$.

nodes.name: Matrix series solution of the system
nodes.statement: The solution is \begin{equation} Y(x) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Solution is $\left(I+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^n(A+Bq^{n-j})\right)Y_0$.

nodes.name: Matrix Ramanujan function $\overline{\mathcal{R}}(A,B,q,xI)$
nodes.statement: We denote this series by \begin{equation} \overline{\mathcal{R}}(A, B, q, xI) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Names the matrix-argument series solving the DDE system $\overline{\mathcal{R}}(A,B,q,xI)$.

nodes.name: Convergence of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: If $0<q<1$, and $(A+Bq^n)$ is invertible for each $n$, then the power series \begin{equation} \overline{\mathcal{R}}(A, B, q, xI) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0, \end{equation} where $A\in M_{n\times n}$ and $B\in M_{n\times n}$ is convergent for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: The matrix Ramanujan series converges on all of $\mathbb{R}$ when each $A+Bq^n$ is invertible.
assumptions: where $A\in M_{n\times n}$ and $B\in M_{n\times n}$

nodes.name: Proof of convergence of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: By ratio test \cite{Lucas}, \begin{eqnarray*} &&\left\|\left(\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\|\\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\|\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\| \\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\| A + Bq^n\right\|\\ &=& 0,\quad \textrm{as}\;n \longrightarrow \infty. \end{eqnarray*} $\therefore$ The power series (\ref{7.2.4}) is convergent for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix ratio test: the successive-term norm ratio equals $\frac{|x|}{n+1}\|A+Bq^n\|\to0$.

nodes.name: Form the matrix ratio
nodes.statement: By ratio test \cite{Lucas}, \begin{eqnarray*} &&\left\|\left(\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\|\\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\|\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\| \\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\| A + Bq^n\right\|\\ &=& 0,\quad \textrm{as}\;n \longrightarrow \infty. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the norm ratio of consecutive terms and simplify to $\frac{|x|}{n+1}\|A+Bq^n\|$.

nodes.name: Conclude convergence
nodes.statement: $\therefore$ The power series (\ref{7.2.4}) is convergent for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude convergence for all real $x$.

nodes.name: Invertibility condition for the matrix analogues
nodes.statement: \par We get following analogous properties and relations as in Section \ref{Prop} under the condition that $A$, $B$, $A\pm I$ and $B\pm I$ are invertible.
nodes.statement_short: The matrix analogues of the Section 5 properties hold provided $A$, $B$, $A\pm I$, $B\pm I$ are invertible.

nodes.name: Matrix scaling property with $A=0$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(0,\pm B^m,q,xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(0,I,q,\pm B^mx\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix analogue of the $a=0$ scaling property.

nodes.name: Matrix scaling property with equal coefficient matrices
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A^m, A^m,q,xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I,I,q,A^mx\right)$, etc.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix analogue of the equal-parameter normalization.

nodes.name: Matrix contiguous relation in $A$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I, B, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1} B, q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix analogue of the contiguous relation shifting $A$ by $\pm I$.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I, B, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1} B, q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.

nodes.name: Matrix contiguous relation in $B$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A, B\pm I, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, A^{-1}(B \pm I), q, Ax\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix analogue of the contiguous relation shifting $B$ by $\pm I$.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A, B\pm I, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, A^{-1}(B \pm I), q, Ax\right)$.

nodes.name: Matrix contiguous relation in both $A$ and $B$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I,, B\pm I, q, xI \right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}} \left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1}(B \pm I), q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix analogue of the contiguous relation shifting both matrices.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I,, B\pm I, q, xI \right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}} \left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1}(B \pm I), q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.

nodes.name: Summary of contributions
nodes.statement: In this article, we have presented a series solution for a differential equation with proportional delay. It is shown that the series is analytical on $\mathbb{R}$. The novel function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)$ is independent from hypergeometric functions because it is obtained as a solution of DDE where as hypergeometric functions are obtained from ODEs. It is observed that the $n^\textrm{th}$ derivative of this function can be represented as the linear combination of $ \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x)$ for $0\leq r \leq n$ with Gaussian binomial coefficients. The function $\mathcal{R}$ is shown to be bounded by exponential functions. The new function $\mathcal{R}$ shows relation with Kummer's functions, with generalized Laguerre polynomials and with incomplete gamma function when integrated with a kernel $e^{-t}$. Further, we have discussed some identities and contiguous relations of $\mathcal{R}$. We also have generalized this function by solving fractional order DDE and a system of DDEs. We hope that our work will encourage researchers to dig for more properties of this new function and to work on DDEs with proportional delay.
nodes.statement_short: Summarizes: $\mathcal{R}$ is entire, its derivatives combine $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)$ with Gaussian binomial weights, it is exponentially bounded, relates to Kummer/Laguerre/incomplete-gamma functions, and generalizes to fractional and matrix settings.
